title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
authors: Vipin Kurian Elavunkel, Sylvain Le Tonquesse, Hadrien Vroylandt
abstract: Identifying earth-abundant catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a central challenge in scalable green hydrogen production. We present a computational pipeline that couples diffusion-based generative modelling, machine-learning force-field relaxation, and graph neural network (GNN) property prediction to discover bimetallic HER catalysts beyond the structures and stoichiometries covered by existing adsorption databases. A generative model (MatterGen) is fine-tuned on bulk alloy structures labelled with their minimum hydrogen adsorption energy and steered towards adsorption energies near zero. From the generated pool we retain the stable structures that are novel bimetallic alloys: binary compositions built from the training-set metals but at stoichiometries or structures absent from that database. Each candidate's low-index facets are ranked by a machine-learning-force-field (MatterSim) surface-energy screen, and only the most stable terminations are converted into explicit slab models with hydrogen adsorbed at all high-symmetry surface sites and relaxed with the same force field. Two GNN surrogates (MEGNet and ALIGNN), trained on a high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) dataset, then screen the resulting slab candidates. Because the two models encode the local environment through different inductive biases, we retain only the alloys on which both agree, reducing the influence of any single model. This consensus screening, combined with a MatterSim energy-difference triangulation, resulted in a shortlist of near-thermoneutral bimetallic candidates. Eight are validated with plane-wave DFT, and four of them, Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3, bind hydrogen within the thermoneutral window. All eight alloys are dynamically stable by phonon calculations. These four alloys are highlighted as DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates for experimental follow-up.

infographic.key_insight: A generative-design and consensus-GNN pipeline identified four DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates with near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding: Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow focuses costly DFT validation on promising alloy structures and stoichiometries beyond those represented in the training database.
method: Fine-tune MatterGen on adsorption-labelled bulk alloys to generate novel bimetallic candidates targeting near-zero hydrogen adsorption energy.
Use MatterSim to screen facet stability and relax hydrogen-decorated slabs at high-symmetry adsorption sites.
Combine MEGNet–ALIGNN consensus with MatterSim energy-difference checks, then validate shortlisted alloys using DFT and phonons.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of eight DFT-tested alloys, four met the thermoneutral hydrogen-binding window; phonon calculations indicated dynamic stability for all eight.
infographic.watch_item: Computed hydrogen binding and dynamic stability do not establish practical HER performance or earth abundance; experimental validation is needed, and all four highlighted candidates contain precious metals.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction

title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
authors: Xuwei Liu, Zhimin Zhang, Xiaoguang Hu, Zhongwei Liu, Yuanhui Sun, Jun Huo
abstract: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

infographic.key_insight: PaddleMaterials unifies six materials-learning task classes in one toolkit while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can connect materials discovery and characterization workflows and enable compiled execution through one setting without changing model definitions.
method: Unify data processing, training, evaluation and pretrained-model management across six task classes.
Record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references for verifiable cross-task composition.
Use a shared compiler backend for graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compilation accelerated every instance in eight groups; LiMnO2 formation-energy predictions were within 7 meV/atom of same-geometry PBE+U references, with model-step costs below one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation.
infographic.watch_item: Universal acceleration was reported for eight of eleven model groups, so speedups should be validated for the intended model and hardware.
infographic.paper_title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science

title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
authors: YuJie Liu, Dezhen Xue, Jun Sun, Xiangdong Ding, Zhibin Gao, Turab Lookman
abstract: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

infographic.key_insight: General-purpose LLMs outperform domain-specific pretrained models in the reported alloy-property benchmarks, with further gains from prior-model numerical estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining general-purpose LLMs with existing predictors and carefully selected reference data could reduce the cost of alloy-property screening.
method: Benchmark general-purpose LLMs against SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT across Ti, steel, HEA, and Al datasets.
Prompt DeepSeek V3.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash with CatBoost or SteelBERT estimates to guide prediction corrections.
Assess similarity-based reference selection and compare self-reported confidence with prediction error.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that using only 5% of high-similarity training references achieves performance comparable to using the full training set.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify errors or out-of-distribution severity, so robustness to substantially different alloy compositions remains unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction

title: An All-Atom Model of the Resorcinol-Formaldehyde Aerogel Skeleton from DFT and Molecular Dynamics: Validation and Iron Incorporation
authors: Shoeb Athar, Jérémy Guazzagaloppa, Philippe Jund
abstract: Resorcinol-formaldehyde (RF) aerogels are lightweight, ultra-porous thermal superinsulators whose complex amorphous structure has not yet been described at the all-atom level. Here, we build an all-atom model of the RF aerogel skeleton by combining density functional theory (DFT) and classical molecular dynamics (MD), validate it against experimental infrared and density measurements, and use it to study the incorporation of iron dopants. The RF base unit was optimized with Gaussian, DMol$^{3}$ and SIESTA, and its calculated infrared spectrum agreed with experiment. Comparing classical force fields with DFT for branched systems of two to four base units (140-278 atoms) led to the choice of COMPASS II. A 15,012-atom system of 54 branched RF units, not cross-linked to each other, aggregated into a single cluster in the canonical (NVT) ensemble and reached an equilibrium density of 1.296 g.cm$^{-3}$ in the isobaric-isothermal (NPT) ensemble, in agreement with the experimental skeletal density (1.3 g.cm$^{-3}$). Then, 5 wt$\%$ iron (109 atoms) was added to the equilibrated structure: during 1 ns of NPT simulation, the fraction of iron atoms embedded in the skeleton rose from 63$\%$ to 71$\%$, and the Fe-C radial distribution function peaked at 3 Å. The model thus provides an experimentally supported starting point for screening fillers and dopants in RF gels, with prospective application to their thermoelectric functionalization, which we have previously demonstrated experimentally with basalt and PANOX fibres. Future extensions could address skeleton properties relevant to thermal insulation and the pyrolysis of RF gels into carbon and metal-doped carbon aerogels.

infographic.key_insight: A DFT-informed all-atom model reproduces the skeletal density of resorcinol-formaldehyde aerogels and tracks iron incorporation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model provides a starting point for screening fillers and dopants for RF aerogels, with potential applications in thermoelectric functionalization and thermal insulation.
method: Optimize the RF base unit with DFT and compare its infrared spectrum with experiment.
Benchmark classical force fields against DFT for branched RF units, selecting COMPASS II.
Simulate a 15,012-atom RF system using NVT and NPT molecular dynamics, then add 5 wt% iron.
infographic.evidence_signal: The calculated infrared spectrum agreed with experiment, the simulated skeletal density was 1.296 versus 1.3 g/cm³ experimentally, and embedded iron increased from 63% to 71% during 1 ns of NPT simulation.
infographic.watch_item: The branched RF units were not cross-linked to one another, so the model does not yet establish the behavior of a fully connected aerogel network.
infographic.paper_title: An All-Atom Model of the Resorcinol-Formaldehyde Aerogel Skeleton from DFT and Molecular Dynamics: Validation and Iron Incorporation

title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
authors: Junchi Liu, Haoran Si, Luo Yan, Sergei Tretiak, Liujiang Zhou
abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: ST2M uses crystal symmetry to guide generation, improving the joint yield of stable, unique, and novel structures under prescribed crystallographic constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry-constrained generation could focus computational screening on viable crystal candidates and accelerate materials discovery.
method: Represent crystals as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits.
Condition discrete–continuous diffusion on Wyckoff patterns and apply degree-of-freedom masks.
Use a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: ST2M reports 96.37% structural validity and a 23.86% stable–unique–novel yield for known patterns, a 68.15% relative gain over the best baseline; first-principles calculations identify 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected low-predicted-energy candidates.
infographic.watch_item: First-principles validation covers selected candidates, and the abstract does not quantify performance on unknown Wyckoff patterns.
infographic.paper_title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation

title: Atomistic Insights into MOCVD Growth of GaAs using a Closed Loop Autonomous System Combining Directed Reinforcement Learning and Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations
authors: Hrishi V. Harsora, Ashutosh Krishna Amaram, Raghavan Ranganathan, Tarun K. Agarwal
abstract: Conventional process optimization of the Metal-Organic Chemical Vapor Deposition (MOCVD) growth parameters to achieve high-quality thin films relies on iterative, resource-intensive experimental runs. While predictive modeling can circumvent this cost and effort, simulating thin-film growth is constrained by the vastly different length and time scales of the deposition process. While continuum (e.g., Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)) and first-principles methods (e.g., Molecular Dynamics (MD)) struggle to balance experimental length/time scales and atomistic accuracy, Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) bridges this divide by resolving atomistic events whilst remaining tractable at experimental length and time scales. However, the accuracy of KMC relies on kinetic rate parameters that require costly density functional theory (DFT) calculations. In order to circumvent this, we present a framework that calibrates the rate parameters directly against experimental growth data. A forward KMC growth model is coupled in a closed loop with a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) optimizer that navigates the high-dimensional parameter space, with the search steered by the degree of rate control of each reaction rate parameter. The approach invokes no material-specific assumptions and hence, any deposition process whose forward kinetics can be reduced to a set of rate-controlled events is amenable to the same treatment. We demonstrate it for the MOCVD of GaAs, where the calibrated model captures the characteristic temperature dependence of the measured growth rate. The framework is also able to recover the three well known kinetic regimes characterized by change in the rate determining step from precursor chemisorption to desorption. As a result, the framework converts routinely measured growth data into a mechanistically interpretable model of the deposition process.

infographic.key_insight: A closed-loop optimizer calibrates atomistic Kinetic Monte Carlo reaction rates directly from experimental GaAs growth data, reducing reliance on costly DFT calculations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework turns routine deposition measurements into a mechanistically interpretable model that could support MOCVD process optimization.
method: Simulate thin-film growth using atomistic Kinetic Monte Carlo.
Use Monte Carlo Tree Search to calibrate kinetic rate parameters against experimental growth data.
Guide parameter search using each reaction’s degree of rate control.
infographic.evidence_signal: For GaAs MOCVD, the calibrated model captures the measured growth-rate dependence on temperature and recovers three known kinetic regimes with changing rate-determining steps.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish parameter uniqueness or predictive accuracy outside the calibration conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic Insights into MOCVD Growth of GaAs using a Closed Loop Autonomous System Combining Directed Reinforcement Learning and Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations

title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications
authors: MD Tanzib Ehsan Sanglap, Ans Al Rashid, Abdullah Sayam, Injamamul Arief, Andrei G. Shvarts, Lukasz Kaczmarczyk
abstract: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency mechanical energy into electricity and enable self-powered sensing. Their performance depends on interactions among material properties, surface morphology, contact mechanics, charge generation and external circuits. This review examines these interactions across length scales to assess how material and interface descriptions support predictive device design. Polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials are discussed in relation to charge generation and retention, mechanical compliance, durability and application requirements. Modelling approaches span molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations, rough-surface contact mechanics, device-scale electrostatics and equivalent circuits. Their capabilities are assessed through the inputs they require, the quantities they predict and the experimental evidence used for validation. Particular attention is given to prescribed surface charge density, idealised geometries and nominal contact-area assumptions, which constrain predictions under realistic loading conditions. Applications are organised by macroscale, milliscale and microscale device dimensions to examine requirements for materials, architecture and integration. The review identifies evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay as critical links between interfacial behaviour and electrical output. A staged validation strategy is proposed for contact mechanics, electrostatics and circuit response, with independent testing beyond calibration conditions. These priorities guide the development of multiscale models and reliable TENG systems.

infographic.key_insight: Predictive triboelectric nanogenerator design requires linking evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay to electrical output across length scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These links can guide material selection, device architecture and circuit integration for mechanical energy harvesting and self-powered sensing.
method: Review polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials against charge retention, compliance and durability requirements.
Assess molecular, contact-mechanics, electrostatic and circuit models by their inputs, predictions and validation evidence.
Organise applications by device scale and propose staged validation with independent testing beyond calibration conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a review of modelling capabilities and experimental validation evidence, but reports no quantitative benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: Prescribed surface charge density, idealised geometries and nominal contact-area assumptions can limit predictions under realistic loading.
infographic.paper_title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications

title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials
authors: Denisse Córdova Carrizales, Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk, L. Dagny Davis, Jeremy Ramsey, Ryotaro Okabe, Mouyang Cheng
abstract: Spatially programmed functional materials, from functionally graded alloys and metamaterials to quantum superlattices, use their spatial structure to tailor physical properties. However, translating a desired spatial structure into a practical fabrication recipe remains challenging due to the complex relationship between processing conditions and resulting material structures. Here we show that a large language model (LLM) agent can inverse-design such fabrication recipes by using a physics-based simulator of ion-matter interactions as a tool. Given an arbitrary depth profile of implanted ions or vacancies, the agent selects the ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers; writes, runs, and interprets simulations; and iteratively refines the recipe until the simulated profile matches the target, with minimal human input. Our work demonstrates physics-guided agentic inverse design as a practical approach to making the spatial structure of materials a programmable variable, opening new opportunities to explore emergent physical phenomena and functional phases of matter.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM agent uses physics-based simulations to inverse-design fabrication recipes for desired depth profiles of implanted ions or vacancies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help translate spatial material designs into ion-processing recipes for graded materials, metamaterials, and quantum superlattices.
method: Specify a target ion or vacancy depth profile.
Let the agent select ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers.
Run and interpret ion–matter simulations, then iteratively refine the recipe.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation-based matching of target profiles with minimal human input, but provides no quantitative accuracy metrics or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical fabrication requires validating simulated profiles against experiments and equipment constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials

title: Complex Martensitic Microstructures in ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$
authors: John M. Ball, Francesco Della Porta, Tomonari Inamura
abstract: We analyze the unusual microstructure resulting from the cubic to orthorhombic phase transformation in the shape-memory alloy ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$. This seems to represent an approximate experimental realization of a deformation having a finite number of incompatible deformation gradients, which has been known to exist only as a theoretical possibility. Because the middle eigenvalue $γ$ of the transformation strain is very close to 1, the phase transformation in this alloy takes place via nucleation of exact austenite-martensite interfaces rather than, as usual for other alloys, by classical austenite-martensite interfaces separating the austenite from a finely-twinned laminate of martensite. According to the moving mask approximation of Della Porta this leads to the question whether a microstructure can be formed from the set $H$ of the twelve matrices ${\mathbf V}_i$ on the martensite energy wells that are rank-one connected to the identity, even though these matrices are mutually incompatible. We show that when $γ=1$ and the transformation is volume preserving, such a microstructure is possible that does not deform the grain boundary. This is a consequence of $H$ forming a degenerate $T_{12}$ configuration in the sense of Kirchheim. In fact there are such microstructures supported on just 8 of the 12 matrices in $H$. However there is no deformation satisfying the same boundary condition whose gradient belongs to $H$ almost everywhere. An additional prediction, confirmed experimentally, is that the macroscopic deformation gradient equals the identity everywhere. We also analyse the approximate compatibility of the ${\mathbf V}_i$. Although mutually incompatible, they are nearly compatible, with some pairs much more nearly compatible than others, these pairs corresponding to interfaces that are more frequently observed.

infographic.key_insight: In Ti₇₆Nb₂₂Al₂, mutually incompatible martensitic deformation gradients can support a boundary-preserving microstructure through a degenerate T₁₂ configuration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis links transformation-strain compatibility to interface formation and macroscopic shape preservation in a shape-memory alloy.
method: Apply the moving mask approximation to 12 martensitic gradients rank-one connected to austenite.
Establish a degenerate T₁₂ configuration under unit middle eigenvalue and volume preservation, with microstructures supported on only 8 gradients.
Analyze near-compatibility between gradient pairs and relate it to observed interfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental confirmation of the predicted identity macroscopic deformation gradient and more frequent observation of interfaces between more nearly compatible pairs.
infographic.watch_item: The construction assumes exact unit middle eigenvalue and volume preservation; no deformation with the same boundary condition has its gradient in the finite set almost everywhere.
infographic.paper_title: Complex Martensitic Microstructures in ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$

title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials
authors: Eliane Younes, Elie Hachem, Marc Bernacki
abstract: Grain growth during heat treatment strongly affects the microstructure of polycrystalline materials and, consequently, their mechanical properties. Although numerical methods such as front-tracking or front-capturing simulations can accurately describe grain growth, their high computational cost limits their use for long or non-isothermal thermal cycles. In previous work, grain growth was successfully predicted under isothermal conditions by treating grain size distributions as time series and forecasting their evolution using recurrent neural networks, allowing complete grain growth trajectories to be generated in seconds rather than through costly PDE-based simulations. In the present work, this forecasting framework is reformulated to handle non-isothermal conditions by explicitly incorporating thermal information into the model architecture. Grain size distributions are encoded using a convolutional neural network, thermal descriptors are embedded through a dedicated multilayer perceptron, and temporal evolution is predicted using a recurrent network. Instantaneous temperature and thermal rate are provided at each time step, allowing the model to adapt its predictions to changing thermal conditions. The framework is trained and evaluated on datasets generated from validated front-tracking simulations across a wide range of non-isothermal thermal paths. The results show that the thermally conditioned model accurately reproduces grain growth dynamics under complex thermal histories, achieving, in k-fold cross-validation over all simulations, mean relative errors of 2.99% (one-hour cycles) and 4.51% (four-hour cycles) with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.99, and mean relative errors between 1.91% and 14.66% on ten simulations following four unseen thermal histories of increasing complexity.

infographic.key_insight: Conditioning recurrent forecasts on temperature and thermal rate enables accurate prediction of grain size distribution evolution during non-isothermal heat treatment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a computationally efficient route to predicting heat-treatment-driven microstructure evolution without repeatedly running costly grain-growth simulations.
method: Encode grain size distributions with a convolutional neural network.
Embed instantaneous temperature and thermal rate with a dedicated multilayer perceptron.
Forecast temporal evolution with a recurrent network trained on validated front-tracking simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all simulations, k-fold cross-validation yielded mean relative errors of 2.99% for one-hour cycles and 4.51% for four-hour cycles, with R² > 0.99; ten simulations spanning four unseen thermal histories yielded errors of 1.91–14.66%.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is simulation-based, and the wider error range on unseen thermal histories warrants caution when extrapolating to new processing conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials

title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery
authors: Aditya Raghavan, Sergei V Kalinin
abstract: Structure property prediction is a classical task in machine learning, ranging from molecular activity and materials properties to local functional responses measured in microscopy. For image-based regression, two choices define the information available to the predictor: the size of the image neighborhood and the spatial resolution retained within it. A small neighborhood can omit relevant surrounding structure, whereas a large, finely sampled neighborhood can introduce redundant or irrelevant information. Here, we develop a framework for constructing spatial descriptors for prediction of local spectra and hysteresis loops. We benchmark regression models, use SHAP maps to examine their spatial attribution, and explore the effect of the patch size and compression to establish the relationship between predictive accuracy and descriptor dimensionality. We then use a genetic algorithm to optimize spatial partitions and the assignment of mean, minimum, and maximum pooling operations. Each retained region contributes an explicit measurement of the image, allowing the search to balance prediction error against the number of descriptor values. Cartesian and polar constructions provide complementary ways to organize this information. The resulting descriptors make it possible to examine where spatial detail is needed, where regional summaries are sufficient, and how these choices depend on the predictor and the measured response. The same approach can be used for molecules and solids once the genetic algorithm rules for these are established.

infographic.key_insight: Genetic algorithms optimize interpretable spatial descriptors to balance local-response prediction error against descriptor size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps identify where detailed image structure or compact regional summaries are needed to predict local spectra and hysteresis loops.
method: Benchmark regression models and examine spatial attribution with SHAP maps.
Evaluate how image patch size and compression affect prediction accuracy and descriptor dimensionality.
Evolve Cartesian or polar spatial partitions with mean, minimum, and maximum pooling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes regression benchmarking and descriptor trade-off evaluations but reports no numerical performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Extension to molecules and solids requires domain-specific genetic algorithm rules that are not established here.
infographic.paper_title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery

title: Temperature-Dependent Ion Dynamics in Argyrodite Superionic Conductor Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl with Fine-Tuned MACE Foundation Model
authors: Jack Yang, Lei Ao, Sean Li
abstract: The rapid growth of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP), particularly the foundational models for materials chemistry, such as MACE, has significantly strengthened our capabilities in studying the complex dynamics of materials through statistical sampling. Here, by performing molecular dynamics with a fine-tuned MACE model, that are further combined with essential dynamics analysis, a tool that is commonly applied in (bio)molecular simulations, we examine the temperature-dependent ion dynamics in a prototypical inorganic solid superionic conductor, namely argyrodite Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl. Our analyses show clear localised phonon-like dynamics for Li$^+$ ions below 500 K with trajectories lying in a low-dimensional manifold that is highly nonlinear, which is opposite to the case in the high-temperature ($\sim$800 K) end. Between 500-700 K, the system exhibit strong competition in the dynamics between the Li$^+$ and framework ions, that are reflected in both the eigenspectrum and the projected low-dimensional embeddings characterising these dynamics not showing a simple monotonic dependency upon rising temperatures, and is further supported by investigations employing Langevin dynamics that systematically examine how damping the framework motions affects the dynamics of the Li$^+$ ions, thanks to the computational efficiency provided by MLIP. This work thus contributes towards the broader theoretical and data-driven framework for studying the lattice dynamics of solids.

infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuned MACE simulations reveal a shift from localized, phonon-like Li⁺ motion below 500 K to contrasting high-temperature dynamics near 800 K, with strong Li⁺–framework competition at 500–700 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding temperature-dependent coupling between lithium and framework motion can inform the design of solid electrolytes for solid-state batteries.
method: Run molecular dynamics of argyrodite Li₆PS₅Cl using a fine-tuned MACE interatomic potential.
Analyze collective ion motion through essential dynamics, eigenspectra, and low-dimensional embeddings.
Use Langevin dynamics to test how damping framework motion affects Li⁺ dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eigenspectra and projected embeddings show nonmonotonic temperature dependence at 500–700 K, with framework-damping simulations supporting competition between Li⁺ and framework dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report quantitative model-accuracy benchmarks or experimental validation, limiting assessment of predictive reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Temperature-Dependent Ion Dynamics in Argyrodite Superionic Conductor Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl with Fine-Tuned MACE Foundation Model

title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys
authors: Eric A. Lass, Carla Joyce C. Nocheseda, Christopher Tandoc, Yong-Jie Hu, Peter K. Liaw
abstract: Refractory compositionally complex alloys (R-CCAs) show great promise as next generation structural materials for extreme conditions, but alloys with excellent high temperature mechanical properties most often exhibit virtually zero room temperature tensile ductility, hindering potential commercial application. Several semi-empirical metrics have been employed for predicting plasticity in R-CCAs, including valence electron concentration, Pugh ratio, Rice criteria, and the D-parameter. While many currently available ductility metrics correlate very well when compressive plasticity is considered, only the density functional theory (DFT) based D-parameter shows a strong correlation in tension. A new ductility metric is developed using CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) thermodynamics, Gamma, with includes the free energy difference between the body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases, the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface, and an electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion. The Gamma parameter exhibits better correlation with tensile ductility than D-parameter and performs equally well in compression. While this improvement is modest, a thermodynamically grounded ductility metric is clearly required to capture intrinsic ductility behavior. Extrinsic contributions to brittle behavior in R-CCAs, namely interstitial oxygen content, are also briefly discussed. Combining the Gamma ductility parameter with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility is proposed as a first order attempt to capture both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to ductile behavior in R-CCAs.

infographic.key_insight: The thermodynamics-based Gamma metric correlates better with tensile ductility in refractory compositionally complex alloys than the DFT-based D-parameter, while performing equally well in compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Gamma could help screen refractory alloys for room-temperature ductility alongside their high-temperature structural performance.
method: Develop Gamma using CALPHAD thermodynamics.
Combine the BCC–HCP free-energy difference, BCC (110) surface interfacial free energy, and electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion.
Compare ductility correlations with existing semi-empirical metrics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a modest improvement in tensile-ductility correlation over the D-parameter and comparable performance in compression, but provides no numerical evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: Gamma addresses intrinsic ductility; incorporating oxygen-related embrittlement through CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility remains a proposed first-order extension.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys

title: Hard to Fool: A Bounded LLM Research Loop for Quantitative Finance, and What Two Dozen Campaigns Found
authors: Henry Zhang
abstract: Agentic research loops that let a language model propose a change, run a fixed experiment and keep whatever improves the metric work well in machine learning. In trading research the same loop is a machine for producing false discoveries: a backtest that "improves the metric" is, by default, overfit, look-ahead, a multiple-comparisons artifact, cost-free, or market drift wearing a strategy. We describe Autonomous Quant Researcher, an open-source loop built on the opposite premise: the model proposes, and only trusted code decides. Proposals are strict declarative JSON over a fixed vocabulary, so there is no model-written code to sandbox. Evaluation runs on immutable chronological stores split into discovery, validation and a final holdout that can be opened exactly once, after a durable receipt is written. Acceptance is a conjunction of absolute gates (positive edge and net P&L after costs, a positive weekly-cluster bootstrap lower bound, survival at elevated costs, per-year stability and sample floors), never a single score. Duplicates are refused before they spend a trial, and every formulation, refusal, crash and result is kept in a hash-chained, append-only ledger. We report every campaign run to date, across 0DTE options priced from traded option bars, overnight SPX verticals, daily ETF rules, technical-analysis premises, Kalshi crypto binaries, earnings options, off-exchange volume and a pre-registered alternative-data campaign. Most hypotheses fail, and we report them. Two results survive their pre-registered bars. The clearest example of the loop working is a failure: a language-model survivor that passed discovery and validation with Sharpe ratios near 3 and fell to 0.26 on its single holdout use. The value of such a loop lies less in what it finds than in how hard it is to make it report something that is not there.

infographic.key_insight: In quantitative finance—not materials discovery—a bounded LLM research loop prioritizes rejecting false discoveries over maximizing backtest performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture illustrates how trusted evaluation code, restricted proposals and auditable records can constrain AI-driven experimental search.
method: Limit model proposals to declarative JSON over a fixed vocabulary; trusted code runs evaluations.
Separate immutable data into discovery, validation and a one-use final holdout.
Require multiple acceptance gates, reject duplicates and log proposals, refusals, crashes and results in a hash-chained ledger.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across roughly two dozen finance campaigns, two results survived pre-registered bars, while one candidate with discovery and validation Sharpe ratios near 3 dropped to 0.26 on holdout.
infographic.watch_item: Passing historical gates does not establish future profitability; market drift remains a concern.
infographic.paper_title: Hard to Fool: A Bounded LLM Research Loop for Quantitative Finance, and What Two Dozen Campaigns Found

title: Data-driven candidate structure ensemble generation beyond the convex hull with crystALL approach
authors: Adam M. Krajewski, Ricardo Amaral, Jonathan W. Siegel, Luke A. Myers, Rushi Gong, Shun-Li Shang
abstract: Real materials consist of multiple stable or metastable states under real-world conditions, existing as statistical ergodic ensembles of configurations rather than ideal crystals. Yet, data-driven computational materials discovery increasingly biases itself toward finding "new stable structures" from ground-state DFT calculations alone. This limits our long-term ability to discover materials whose properties emerge from metastable phases, to explain experimental observations, or to model thermodynamic behavior comprehensively. Predicting ergodic sets of atomic configurations of known and hypothetical solids is a fundamental challenge in theoretical crystallography, approached via many complementary methods. We discuss this conceptually and introduce crystALL, a pragmatic and powerful data-driven approach to discovering ensembles beyond the convex hull, embracing structural diversity over stability alone, enabling robust experiment matching in cases evading traditional methods. crystALL leverages 5 million relaxed structures from OPTIMADE and MPDD to rapidly generate a comprehensive candidate set by: (1) species substitutions; (2) ML feature-space analysis with pySIPFENN; (3) representative structure selection via clustering and energy-minimization or property matching; and (4) construction of the final candidate ensemble for experimental or ab initio validation. We also uniquely address the common challenge of experimental composition uncertainties spanning many integer stoichiometries by new efficient searches across anonymized compositional ranges rather than fixed formulas. Overall, crystALL's ensemble-focused philosophy provides critical advantages over the prevailing convex-hull-searching paradigm, which often fails to account for key experimental observations and increases AI/ML discovery bias over time - akin to model collapse in LLMs retrained on iteratively generated content.

infographic.key_insight: crystALL generates diverse candidate crystal ensembles beyond the convex hull, prioritizing stable and metastable structures rather than ground-state stability alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Broader candidate ensembles can help engineers interpret experimental phases and investigate materials whose properties depend on metastable configurations.
method: Generate candidates through species substitutions, including searches across anonymized composition ranges.
Analyze candidates in ML feature space using pySIPFENN and cluster them to select representatives.
Use energy minimization or property matching to assemble ensembles for experimental or ab initio validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach draws on 5 million relaxed structures from OPTIMADE and MPDD; the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy or runtime benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Candidate diversity does not establish thermodynamic populations or kinetic accessibility; downstream validation remains necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven candidate structure ensemble generation beyond the convex hull with crystALL approach

title: Statistically Robust Characterization of Polaron and Bipolaron Intrinsic Traps in Amorphous Silica Reveals the Role of Network Flexibility in Electron Localisation
authors: Robin Delhomme, Jonathon Cottom, Emilia Olsson
abstract: Intrinsic electron localization in amorphous silica (a-SiO2) contributes to charge trapping and defect generation in silica-based electronic materials - a phenomenon that degrades logic-device performance but can be exploited for memory applications. However, the structural distribution of one- and two-electron traps remains incompletely characterized, largely because the disordered covalent network of a-SiO2 spans a vast configurational space. To address this, we perform statistical sampling to select a representative 200-model subset of defect-free bulk a-SiO2 structures from a structurally converged parent set of 2512 models, generated via classical melt-quench molecular dynamics simulations. We then characterize the intrinsic one- and two-electron traps in this subset using HSE06 density functional theory calculations. Analysis of neutral precursor sites shows that trapping propensity is not determined by a universal O-Si-O angle or Si-O bond length; it is controlled by the accessibility of the relaxed trap geometry, requiring both local strain and medium-range network flexibility. Single electrons predominantly form edge-centred polarons on distorted SiO4 tetrahedra, with occupied states 3.1-4.3 eV below the conduction band minimum. Injection of a second electron drives stronger lattice relaxation, most commonly Si-O bond elongation leading to rupture, thereby forming threefold-coordinated-Si (Si3) bipolarons and, in some cases, Si-Si-bonded bipolaron configurations. The calculated bipolaron energy ranges are consistent with optical absorption features at 3.7, 4.7, and 6.4 eV associated with intrinsic electron localization.

infographic.key_insight: Intrinsic electron trapping in amorphous silica depends on local strain and medium-range network flexibility, not a universal bond-length or bond-angle threshold.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding these traps can inform efforts to reduce charge-induced degradation in silica-based logic devices or exploit charge localization in memory applications.
method: Generate 2,512 defect-free amorphous silica models using classical melt-quench molecular dynamics.
Statistically select a representative subset of 200 structures.
Use HSE06 density functional theory to characterize one- and two-electron traps and structural relaxation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the sampled structures, single-electron polarons have occupied states 3.1–4.3 eV below the conduction band minimum, while calculated bipolaron energy ranges are consistent with optical absorption features at 3.7, 4.7, and 6.4 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern simulated defect-free bulk silica; interfaces, pre-existing defects, and device operating conditions may alter trapping behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Statistically Robust Characterization of Polaron and Bipolaron Intrinsic Traps in Amorphous Silica Reveals the Role of Network Flexibility in Electron Localisation

title: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulation with external field
authors: Chengji Li, Fan Zheng
abstract: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations with classical path approximation (CPA-NAMD) cannot simulate the carrier dynamics under an external field. We develop CPA-NAMD-extF, a first-principles density-matrix framework for calculating field-driven electronic responses along precomputed finite-temperature ionic trajectories. The method combines explicit external-field coupling with self-consistent updates of electronic density while retaining the computational efficiency of the classical-path approximation. Benchmarks against regular TDDFT methods show close agreement for time-dependent dipoles, finite-field currents, and linear optical responses. Applications to the linear absorption spectrum of crystalline and amorphous SiO$_2$ demonstrate its capability to large and structurally complex systems. This method is also applied to the 2D hybrid perovskite $(\mathrm{BA})_2\mathrm{CsPb}_2\mathrm{Br}_7$. Finite-temperature calculations show that the second-order opto-current response is strongly affected by structural fluctuations. Real-space DC current density further reveals pronounced Br-centered vortex currents, and its microscopic origin is investigated.

infographic.key_insight: CPA-NAMD-extF extends classical-path nonadiabatic molecular dynamics to field-driven electronic responses, revealing strong structural-fluctuation effects on second-order opto-currents.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables computationally efficient finite-temperature optical and electronic response calculations for large, structurally complex materials.
method: Evolve a first-principles electronic density matrix along precomputed finite-temperature ionic trajectories.
Include explicit external-field coupling and self-consistent electronic-density updates.
Apply the framework to crystalline and amorphous SiO₂ and the 2D hybrid perovskite (BA)₂CsPb₂Br₇.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks show close agreement with regular TDDFT for time-dependent dipoles, finite-field currents, and linear optical responses; perovskite calculations reveal Br-centered vortex currents.
infographic.watch_item: Precomputed ionic trajectories retain the classical-path approximation, so field-induced feedback on ionic motion requires careful assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulation with external field

title: Shock-driven Jetting at HMX Crystal Surface Asperities
authors: Ethan Holbrook, Matthew P. Kroonblawd, H. Keo Springer, Alejandro Strachan
abstract: Shock-induced jetting and recompression are plausible mechanisms for hot spot formation in energetic materials, but remain poorly understood. To this end, we apply all-atom nonreactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of a shock-loaded sinusoidal surface asperity in the crystalline explosive HMX (octahydro-1,3,5,7-tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocine) to quantify the roles of shock strength, asperity geometry, system size, and crystallographic orientation in determining the jetting response. Our simulations span a shock pressure interval of $\approx$4-47 GPa, which captures responses in both detonation initiation and steady-state detonation regimes. We find that shock strength and asperity curvature exert strong influence on jet velocity, temperature, and morphology, while feature size and crystallographic orientation play more modest roles. Jet morphology correlates strongly with the HMX ambient-pressure phase diagram and the narrow temperature range associated with its liquid phase. Coherent jets form when focusing and dissipation are sufficient to drive local temperatures above the melting point, while formation of molecular plumes is seemingly connected to jet temperatures exceeding the liquid-vapor transition temperature. Formation of plumes is unlike the jetting responses seen in metals, which typically exhibit liquid phases that are stable over wider temperature intervals. This work proposes a simple hypothesis for the connection between jet morphology and ambient-pressure phase diagrams that can be readily tested in other explosives and metals. It also provides a foundation for ongoing nonreactive and reactive MD simulations of jet impact and recompression to quantify the role played by jets in forming hot spots in HMX-based explosives.

infographic.key_insight: Shock strength and surface-asperity curvature strongly govern HMX jet velocity, temperature, and morphology, with coherent jets and molecular plumes linked to melting and vaporization, respectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding asperity-driven jetting can help assess potential hot spot formation mechanisms in HMX-based explosives under shock loading.
method: All-atom nonreactive molecular dynamics of shock-loaded sinusoidal HMX surface asperities.
Varied shock strength, asperity geometry, system size, and crystallographic orientation.
Compared jet morphology with the ambient-pressure HMX phase diagram.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations spanning approximately 4–47 GPa found strong effects of shock strength and asperity curvature, but more modest effects of feature size and crystal orientation.
infographic.watch_item: Nonreactive simulations do not capture chemical ignition, and the proposed phase-diagram connection requires testing in other materials.
infographic.paper_title: Shock-driven Jetting at HMX Crystal Surface Asperities

title: Low cross-plane thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films
authors: Seungwon Park, Jingyu Tang, Minsung An, Alan J. H. McGaughey, Lisa M. Porter, Robert F. Davis
abstract: The thermal conductivities of (001) $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films deposited on $c$-plane sapphire substrates were measured with frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR). The thermal conductivity increases from 1.83 $^{+0.19}_{-0.18}$ W/m$\cdot$K to 2.26 $^{+0.35}_{-0.40}$ W/m$\cdot$K as the thicknesses increase from 159 nm to 689 nm. This weak thickness dependence indicates that the majority of the intrinsic phonon mean free paths are smaller than the range of investigated film thicknesses. First-principles-based calculations that include phonon-phonon and phonon-boundary scattering capture this size-dependent behavior and support our experimental observation. Temperature-dependent measurements of a 689 nm film from 293 to 400 K show a decrease in thermal conductivity with increasing temperature due to enhanced phonon-phonon scattering. A weaker temperature dependence is observed in a 159 nm film where phonon-boundary scattering becomes more prominent. At comparable film thicknesses, our measured $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ films exhibit lower values of cross-plane thermal conductivity than the other experimentally measured Ga$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs. Our experimental observations are supported by prior predictions, which suggest that the low thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ results from its complex crystal structure, which leads to increased anharmonicity and lower phonon group velocities relative to other polymorphs. Thermal management strategies, such as integration with high-thermal-conductivity substrates, may thus be required to mitigate self-heating for $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$-based electronic devices.

infographic.key_insight: κ-Ga₂O₃ thin films have low cross-plane thermal conductivity with weak thickness dependence, consistent with most intrinsic phonon mean free paths being shorter than the investigated film thicknesses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: κ-Ga₂O₃ electronics may require high-thermal-conductivity substrates or other heat-removal strategies to mitigate self-heating.
method: Frequency-domain thermoreflectance on (001) κ-Ga₂O₃ films grown on c-plane sapphire.
Thickness-dependent measurements from 159–689 nm and temperature-dependent measurements from 293–400 K.
First-principles-based calculations incorporating phonon–phonon and phonon–boundary scattering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Thermal conductivity increased from 1.83 (+0.19/−0.18) to 2.26 (+0.35/−0.40) W/(m·K) between 159 and 689 nm, with calculations capturing the weak size dependence.
infographic.watch_item: These cross-plane results for sapphire-supported films do not directly establish in-plane heat transport or device-level thermal performance.
infographic.paper_title: Low cross-plane thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films

title: TT-SCHA for Thermodynamics of Binary Alloys
authors: Boian S. Alexandrov, Dimiter Petsev
abstract: The free energy of a crystal is an integral over the positions of all its atoms, in 3N dimensions. We evaluate it without random sampling for the ordered alloys B2 NiAl and gamma-TiAl with embedded-atom potentials, using a self-consistent harmonic approximation (SCHA) corrected to third order in temperature, calculated via thermal averages of tensor-train (TT) integrals built from one atom and its neighbors, which we call TT-SCHA. The result is for an infinite crystal without sampling error; its numerical error is set by the starting pivots of the interpolation (up to 9 MPa in the pressure, reduced by averaging three runs; SM Table S26). Against the molecular dynamics of 65,536 atoms (Frenkel-Ladd free energy at 600 K, integrated energy above), TT-SCHA free energy agrees to 0.13 meV per atom at 600-1000 K, using 420-500 times fewer core-seconds for one run. At zero pressure, results agree with published calculations that use the same embedded-atom potential: the published elastic constants of gamma-TiAl (to 1 GPa, by a static lattice calculation) and its thermal expansion from Monte Carlo sampling (to 0.012 percentage points).

infographic.key_insight: TT-SCHA computes binary-alloy crystal free energies without random sampling, matching molecular dynamics within 0.13 meV per atom at 600–1000 K with 420–500× fewer core-seconds per run.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method could lower the computational cost of predicting alloy thermodynamics, thermal expansion, and elastic properties within embedded-atom potential models.
method: Apply a self-consistent harmonic approximation with corrections through third order in temperature.
Evaluate local thermal averages using tensor-train integrals over one atom and its neighbors.
Obtain infinite-crystal results without finite-size sampling or random-sampling error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on B2 NiAl and γ-TiAl used 65,536-atom molecular dynamics as a free-energy benchmark; zero-pressure γ-TiAl results also matched published same-potential elastic constants within 1 GPa and thermal expansion within 0.012 percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to two ordered alloys with embedded-atom potentials, and interpolation starting pivots introduce numerical pressure errors up to 9 MPa, reduced by averaging three runs.
infographic.paper_title: TT-SCHA for Thermodynamics of Binary Alloys
